case.title: Science fair venue, budget and volunteers

canvasName: R1-C06 Science fair venue, budget and volunteers

segments.text: Thank you for coming to the science fair planning meeting. We have about forty minutes and we need to leave with a budget, a schedule, a venue plan, and named owners. The fair is for grades six through eight, it will run on a Saturday in October, and we expect one hundred and twenty student projects. Last year we had eighty projects and it was already crowded, so this year we need a different layout.
segments.textReply: Captured the fair’s grades, October Saturday timing, expected 120 projects (up from 80), and the need for a new venue layout. The meeting’s target decisions—budget, schedule, venue, and named owners—are also on the board.

segments.text: Let's start with the goal. The fair should be a low pressure opportunity for students to explain their work, not a pure competition. Every student gets a table and a short presentation slot. We will have three judged categories: scientific method, engineering design, and communication. We also want a family open house in the afternoon so parents and younger students can visit.
segments.textReply: I’m adding the student-centered format, judging categories, and afternoon family open house.

segments.text: The venue options are the school gym, the cafeteria plus hallway, and the community college atrium. The gym is free and can hold one hundred and twenty tables, but the acoustics are terrible and the floor is needed for basketball on Friday night, so setup cannot start until seven in the morning.
segments.textReply: I’ll add the three venue options and capture the gym’s capacity, cost, sound, and setup constraint.

segments.text: The cafeteria and hallway can hold ninety tables and setup can start Friday afternoon, but the hallway is a fire lane and we cannot block it. The college atrium is beautiful and has parking, but it costs eight hundred dollars and requires a certificate of insurance. The safety requirements are not optional. Every project using heat, chemicals, or live animals needs a pre approval form signed by a teacher.

The board also records the non-negotiable safety rule: heat, chemical, and live-animal projects require a teacher-signed pre-approval form. No venue has been selected yet.

segments.text: Last year we spent two thousand on tables, six hundred on printing, four hundred on awards, and three hundred on snacks. This year we want to add a keynote speaker and a livestream for families who cannot attend. The speaker honorarium is five hundred, the AV rental is seven hundred, and the livestream requires a volunteer and a dedicated laptop. Let's compare the two realistic venue plans.
segments.textReply: I’ll capture last year’s spending and the proposed keynote/livestream costs, then mark the two-plan comparison as the next agenda stage.Added last year’s $3,300 spending breakdown and the proposed keynote and AV costs. The livestream’s volunteer and dedicated-laptop needs are noted; the two venue plans are queued for comparison.

segments.text: Plan A is the gym plus the outdoor courtyard for food trucks. Capacity is good, setup is painful, and the acoustics are poor. Plan B is the cafeteria, the hallway, and four classrooms for quiet presentations. Capacity is ninety projects, so we would need to limit entries or run two sessions. The college atrium is a third option but the insurance and cost make it a stretch.
segments.textReply: I’m laying out the two workable plans side by side, with the atrium retained as a stretch alternative.Added a side-by-side comparison: Plan A offers capacity but has setup and acoustics drawbacks; Plan B adds quiet rooms but serves only 90 projects unless entries are limited or sessions split. The college atrium remains a costly, insurance-dependent stretch option.

segments.text: The committee's preference is Plan A if we can solve three problems: setup time, noise, and power. The custodial team says they can open the gym at six, not seven, if we submit a request two weeks ahead. The AV club can lend us two portable speakers and six microphones. The facilities team can bring in two quiet generators for the courtyard, but we need to keep them away from the presentation tables.
segments.textReply: Plan A is the committee’s conditional preference; I’m recording the proposed setup, sound, and power mitigations.Added Plan A’s conditional mitigations: request 6 a.m. gym access two weeks ahead, borrow speakers and microphones from the AV club, and place the courtyard generators away from presentation tables.

segments.text: For noise, we will group the noisier engineering projects near the courtyard and keep the reading and communication projects in the quiet corner. We will not use the gym's main sound system for announcements; instead we will use a small PA at the entrance. Presentations will be scheduled in fifteen minute blocks with five minute transitions.
segments.textReply: Adding the noise-zoning strategy, entrance PA choice, and 15-minute presentation blocks with 5-minute transitions.Added the noise zoning and entrance-PA plan, plus 15-minute presentation blocks separated by 5-minute transitions.

segments.text: Judges will rotate in pairs, and each pair will see no more than twelve projects. The schedule is tight. Eight in the morning, student setup. Nine, welcome and safety briefing. Nine thirty to eleven thirty, judging. Eleven thirty to twelve thirty, lunch and family open house. Twelve thirty to two, public viewing and hands on demos. Two to two thirty, keynote. Two thirty to three, awards and cleanup.
segments.textReply: Added the timed Saturday agenda and judging constraint: pairs rotate, with no more than 12 projects per pair.

shapes.title: Science Fair Committee — Meeting Summary
shapes.html:
Science Fair Planning
Purpose: leave with a budget, schedule, venue plan, and named owners for a Saturday-in-October fair serving grades 6–8 and up to 120 projects.
Decisions confirmed
  • Venue: Plan A — school gym + courtyard. Atrium is backup only if gym is unavailable.
  • Format: low-pressure student showcase; each student gets a table and short presentation slot; cap registration at 120.
  • Layout & sound: noisy engineering near courtyard; reading/communication in quiet corner; small entrance PA, not gym system.
  • Budget: approve $3,100 planned spend; hold $900 contingency. PTA covers; receipts within two weeks.
  • Accessibility: temporary ramp at courtyard door; reserve front row for wheelchairs and strollers; ask families about needs at registration.
Program & operating plan
  • Judged categories: scientific method, engineering design, communication; pairs rotate, max 12 projects per pair.
  • Afternoon family open house; keynote, hands-on demos, awards.
  • Presentations: 15-minute blocks + 5-minute transitions; two quiet courtyard generators kept away from tables.
  • Safety: teacher-signed pre-approval for heat, chemical, or live-animal projects; no open flames; grounded outlets only, no daisy-chained strips; 2 first-aid stations and clear emergency access.
  • District safety officer reviews floor plan two weeks before event.

  • Judge threshold conflicts: one point says switch if fewer than 12 judges at T−2 weeks; the final update says fewer than 10 and reduce judging by 30 minutes. Confirm one trigger and the fallback details.
  • Current confirmed volunteers: 6 judges, 2 check-in. Need 12 judges, 4 check-in, 2 first aid, 2 floaters, 1 AV lead. College outreach may send 5 students (service-hours forms needed); ask high-school science club for remaining help.
  • Plan A setup is early: gym opens at 6 a.m. only with advance request; clear venue by 4 p.m. for evening event.
  • Power/noise: keep 2 quiet generators away from presentation tables; ensure electrical and emergency-access controls on floor plan.
  • Livestream funding/cost not specified; fundraising amount also TBD. PTA says it can cover approved spend.
